title: Luca's Fancy Fonts Fiasco
markdown:
The Whispering Creek Fête was nearly here. The whole valley buzzed like a hive ready to share its honey. The air smelled of blooming honeysuckle, a perfume that made whiskers twitch, and of blackberry pie, a scent that made tummies rumble just thinking about it. Luca the raccoon, apprentice at Bartholomew’s Print Shop, had been given the programme — the very map of the day’s delights. Luca loved letters with all his bushy tail. He did not want a programme. He wanted a programme that sang like a thrush at dawn, a programme that sparkled like dew on a spiderweb.

Bartholomew the printer, a badger with ink-stained paws and a kind heart, often praised Luca’s knack for ink and paper. Luca liked things impressive. He rifled through Bartholomew’s vast collection of type, a treasure of metallic letters, each with its own personality. He bypassed the cheerful round letters that looked like friendly pebbles and the neat sensible ones as orderly as ants on a march. His eyes gleamed like polished acorns when he found them: Gilded Griffin, which seemed to drip with ancient importance, as if penned by a king’s scribe, and Majestic Marmot, which looked carved onto old weathered rock by stubborn mountain goats.

“Perfect,” he chittered, heart giving a happy hop, and set to work with gusto.

The simple Bake-Off became A Grand Confectionary Competition of Edible Artistry. The cheerful Three-Legged Race became The Ambling Gauntlet of Synchronised Locomotion. The cozy Storytelling Circle was proudly announced as An Oral Recitation of Fabled Narratives. The whole programme shimmered, in Luca’s opinion, with a refined elegance that would make everyone feel the grandeur of the day. He imagined the gasps of admiration. It looked splendid. It did not look like pie.

On the morning of the fête, sunbeams dappled through the leaves, and the valley echoed with the happy chatter of arriving guests. Luca, puffed with pride, helped Bartholomew hand out the newly printed programmes. He watched with a hopeful gleam as the forest folk received their copies, eager for delighted exclamations.

Tansy the rabbit peered at her page, nose twitching. “Synchronised locomotion?” she murmured to a squirrel whose tail had frozen mid-flick. “Do we have to dance while hopping? All at the same time?”

Old Mr Iestyn Bear, a creature of simple pleasures and a rumbling chuckle, blinked at the Confectionary Competition. “Edible art?” he grumbled. “I just want a slice of pie, not a picture made of pastry. I hope they have custard too.”

Bartholomew’s cousin, Bartholomew the Badger — no relation to the printer, though they both had excellent taste in honey — heard about the Fabled Narratives. He adjusted his spectacles. “Fabled? I hope they are not too frightening. I always preferred cheerful tales about brave little hedgehogs. I think I shall stick to the jams.”

As the fête got underway, confusion bloomed like an unwelcome weed. Young field mice, whiskers quivering, gathered at the Synchronised Locomotion starting line and tried to step in unison on three small feet. Their tiny legs were made for scurrying, not for marches. They wobbled, tripped, and tumbled into a giggling squeaking heap. Luca heard the squeaks, felt the ground vibrate, and smelled the dusty earth kicked up by their paws.

Mrs Cottontail, whose fluffy tail was almost as impressive as her berry pies, stood by her stall looking utterly baffled. The judges, noses buried in the programmes, kept asking if her apple crumble was intended as a metaphorical representation of autumnal transition. She just wanted them to taste it.

“It is just a crumble,” she sighed. “But a very tasty one.”

Luca watched from the print-shop stall. A prickle of unease, like a tiny nettle, ran along his ears, which drooped ever so slightly. The programme was beautiful. The letters were grand. His friends did not look as if they were having fun. They looked confused, a little worried, and not at all as gleeful as they usually were at Whispering Creek. The joyous laughter seemed quieter. The happy hum had a puzzled hole in it. It looked splendid. It did not look like pie.

Aunt June ambled over with a basket of cinnamon buns, her steps unhurried, her scent a comfort. “What troubles you, little raccoon?”

“My programme,” Luca said, voice small. “It is supposed to make everything sound wonderful. They all look bewildered. I used the most distinguished fonts. Bartholomew said they were the very best for important documents.”

Aunt June surveyed the scene. Iestyn Bear attempted to applaud the baker’s artistic endeavours with one hesitant paw. “Distinguished fonts are splendid,” she said. “They have their place, like the old oak. But the fête is not about sounding grand. It is about us, together.” She turned a crisp page. “When you want to share a bun, do you announce A Humble Offering of Baked Flour and Sweetness? Or do you say, with a smile, Bun? Who wants a bun?”

Luca imagined the bun announcement. Cheerful. Inviting. He could almost taste it.

“The grandest words can hide the simplest joys,” Aunt June went on, not as a lecture, but as if she were handing him a warm corner of pastry. “Clear water shows the sky. Fancy letters can make a party sound like a royal decree.”

“Oh,” Luca said. A spark. “I have made it too important.”

“Precisely. You have used your talent to make things sound grand. Sometimes the important thing is to make them sound clear. Now, what can we do to make it fun again?”

Luca scampered to Tansy, who was patiently telling a mole that synchronised locomotion meant running with a friend. “Tansy. We need to fix this.”

Together they hurried to the print shop, paws making soft thuds on the forest floor. Bartholomew, amused by the fuss and seeing the genuine wish to make things right, let them have another go. Luca chose a cheerful clear font this time, one that felt like a friendly smile and was as easy to read as a robin’s song. Bake-Off became simply Best Cakes and Pies. The Ambling Gauntlet of Synchronised Locomotion was rewritten as The Friendly Three-Legged Race, complete with a little drawing of two mice holding paws. The Oral Recitation of Fabled Narratives became the inviting Stories Under the Old Oak.

The press thumped. Ink smelled sharp and hopeful. New programmes were handed out, and a wave of relief and delight swept the fête like a happy breeze. The mice yelped with joy as they tumbled in the race, giggles echoing through the trees. Mrs Cottontail beamed as the judges, now able to understand the simple joy of pie, eagerly sampled her treats and declared them absolutely delicious. Iestyn Bear loudly declared his appreciation for the delicious art and made sure to have a very generous second slice. Bartholomew the Badger happily settled in for a cheerful tale about a brave little hedgehog, and did not once mention fables.

Luca watched, his heart lighter than a dandelion seed on the breeze, bushy tail wagging. He saw his friends laughing, not confused. He heard them sharing stories, not fearing them. It was the same fête, the same sunshine, the same delicious smells, but now everyone understood, and everyone was happy.

It looked simple. It looked like pie. And that, for a programme, was the most beautiful kind of elegance he knew.
characters: Luca (an ink-loving raccoon apprentice), Tansy (a practical rabbit), Aunt June (a cinnamon-bun aunt)
